items.q: What is a context window, and how do you manage it in a long chat?
items.a: The most tokens a model can read in one request (system prompt, tools, messages, reply). Manage it with a **sliding window** of recent turns, **summaries** of older ones, and **long-term facts** fetched when needed.
items.trap: Saying a big window means you never need to manage it: cost and latency grow long before the limit.

items.q: Why can't you just drop the oldest message?
items.a: Because messages come in linked groups. Dropping a `tool_use` but keeping its `tool_result` (or the reverse) makes the request **invalid**. Cut at **turn boundaries** instead.
items.trap: Forgetting that tool results are sent with the user role.

scenes.explain: A window bounds cost, but anything older than the window is gone. Lessons 3 and 4 fix that with summaries and long-term facts.

A conversation grows every turn: cost and latency
Sliding window: keep the last N turns (or a token budget)
Cut at turn starts; tool pairs stay together

captions.text: In lesson one, you saw that a conversation is a list you resend every time, and that
it keeps growing.
In this lesson, you'll measure that growth, learn what the context window is, and
keep the conversation small with a sliding window, without breaking tool calls.
You'll explain tokens, and the context window.
Measure how a conversation grows, turn by turn.
Keep only the last few turns, with a sliding window.
And cut only at turn boundaries, so tool calls stay valid.
First, a picture.
A classroom whiteboard holds only so much writing.
When it's full, the teacher must erase something before writing anything new.
The context window is the model's whiteboard.
It's everything the model can read in one request: the system prompt, the tools, the
messages, and room for its reply.
It's measured in tokens.
A token is a piece of text, a few characters long.
In English, roughly three quarters of a word.
The window size is the most tokens one request can hold.
And you pay for every input token you send, on every call.
Today's Claude models have very large context windows, hundreds of thousands of
tokens.
So why worry?
Because long before you hit the limit, a growing conversation costs more on every
turn, and every reply gets slower.
Let's measure it.
The code is on the left, and its output is on the right.
We build a conversation of five turns.
Each turn is a short question, and a long answer, like real tutoring.
After each turn we print the size.
About a hundred and fifty tokens more every turn.
And remember, the whole thing is sent on every call.
That's the cost of perfect memory.
Now the simplest fix: a sliding window.
We keep only the last two turns.
Four messages, about two hundred and ninety tokens, less than half.
The oldest message kept is: explain loops.
But here's the price.
We ask: what's my name?
And the answer is: I don't know.
The name was in turn one, and turn one slid out of the window.
There are two common ways to size a window.
By turns: keep the last N turns.
It's simple, and easy to reason about.
But one turn with a huge answer can still be too big.
Or by tokens: keep as many recent turns as fit a token budget.
That keeps the size under a known limit.
To count tokens you can estimate, about four characters per token, or ask the API
exactly, with its count tokens endpoint.
Here's the project's version.
First, a rough token estimate: about four characters per token.
Good enough to decide when to trim.
For exact numbers, use the API's count tokens endpoint.
Now, where do developers go wrong?
Cutting in the wrong place.
A turn starts with a user message whose content is plain text.
Tool results are also sent with the user role, but they're a list of blocks, so they
don't start a turn.
The conversation class holds the messages, and a summary we'll use next lesson.
Its size is the estimate of both.
This method finds the index where each turn starts.
And the window starts at the turn start, so many turns back.
That guarantees a tool use block and its tool result are never separated.
Let's dry run it on a chat with a tool call.
Message zero, the user's own words: a turn starts here.
Message one: the assistant asks for a tool.
Message two: the tool result.
User role, but not a turn start.
Message three: the reply.
Message four starts turn two.
With keep turns two, the window starts here.
And everything after it is kept.
Pause and try it.
Here are eight messages.
Message three is a tool use, and message four is its tool result.
Which messages does a window of two turns keep?
Turns start at messages zero, two and six.
Keeping two turns means starting at message two, so it keeps messages two to seven,
and the tool use stays with its result.
Interview corner.
What is a context window, and how do you manage it in a long chat?
A good answer: it's the most tokens a model can read in one request, including the
system prompt, tools, messages and the reply.
You manage it with a sliding window of recent turns, summaries of older turns, and
long-term facts that you fetch when needed.
The trap: saying a big window means you never need to manage it.
Cost and latency grow long before the limit.
Follow-up.
Why can't you just drop the oldest message?
Because messages come in linked groups.
Dropping a tool use but keeping its tool result, or the reverse, makes the request
invalid.
So you cut at turn boundaries.
The trap is forgetting that tool results are sent with the user role, so not every
user message starts a turn.
Quick check.
A sliding window keeps the last three turns.
What's the main risk?
Facts from early turns, like the user's name, are lost.
The window keeps costs down, but forgets.
Let's recap.
The context window is everything one request can hold, measured in tokens.
A conversation grows every turn, which costs money and time.
A sliding window keeps the last few turns, or as many as fit a token budget.
And always cut where a turn starts, so tool pairs stay together.
